longerExplanation: Used to describe a habit or situation that happens often, usually one that is undesirable or problematic. It translates to 'it is common to...' or 'to do [X] more often than not.'

sentenceExamples.en: If you rush, it's common to make mistakes.
He is always (habitually) late for appointments.
In winter, it's very common to catch a cold.

name: -(으)ㄴ/는 법이다
englishMeaning: It's natural that... / It's the law that...
briefDescription: Expresses an inevitable truth. Similar to: -기 마련이다 (No. 71).
featuredTranslation: It is only natural that spring comes when winter goes.
longerExplanation: Used to state a universal rule or principle. It implies that a certain outcome is fixed by nature or logic and cannot be changed. It is a very authoritative and definitive expression.

sentenceExamples.en: The truth is bound to be revealed someday.
It is natural that pleasure follows hardship.
Greed naturally leads to trouble.

name: -(으)ㄹ 바에야
englishMeaning: Rather than... / Since you're doing it anyway...
briefDescription: Used to choose a better option among poor choices. Similar to: -느니 차라리 (No. 118).
featuredExample: 늦을 바에야 안 가는 게 낫겠어요.
featuredTranslation: Rather than going late, it would be better not to go at all.
longerExplanation: This structure compares two options, implying the first is so bad that the second (often extreme) choice is preferable. It can also mean 'since you are already doing [X], you might as well do it right/thoroughly.'

sentenceExamples.kr: 포기할 바에야 죽을 힘을 다해 보세요.
sentenceExamples.en: Rather than giving up, try with all your might.

sentenceExamples.kr: 맛없는 것을 먹을 바에야 그냥 굶겠어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Rather than eating something untasty, I'd rather just starve.

sentenceExamples.kr: 도움을 받을 바에야 혼자 하는 게 편해요.
sentenceExamples.en: Rather than receiving help, it's more comfortable doing it alone.

name: -다 못해
englishMeaning: Can't stand V-ing anymore / Beyond the limit of
briefDescription: Indicates a state has reached an extreme limit. Similar to: -(으)ㄹ 정도로 (No. 18).
featuredTranslation: I couldn't stand waiting any longer, so I left first.
longerExplanation: Used when a condition or action exceeds a threshold. For example, 'too many to count' or 'so sad I couldn't even cry.' It shows that the state in the first clause shifted to an even more extreme or different state in the second clause.

sentenceExamples.en: Beyond being sad, my heart actually hurts.
Beyond just being beautiful, it feels mysterious.
I couldn't hold it in anymore, so I got angry.

name: -(으)ㄴ 끝에
englishMeaning: After a long period of... / At the end of...
briefDescription: Indicates a result achieved after a long struggle. Similar to: -고 나서 (No. 96).
featuredTranslation: After much agonizing, I reached a decision.
longerExplanation: This emphasizes the process and the effort. It's usually used with nouns or verbs describing hardship, thinking, or long actions. It suggests that the final result was finally achieved after going through that process.

sentenceExamples.en: After long effort, they succeeded.
At the end of the meeting, they reached an agreement.
After a fight, they reconciled.

name: -아/어 대다
briefDescription: Repetition of an action, often with a negative nuance. Similar to: -곤 하다 (No. 79).
featuredTranslation: I had a hard time because the child kept crying (intensely).
longerExplanation: This adds a nuance of 'to an excessive degree' or 'annoyingly frequent.' It's often used when the speaker is bothered by someone else's repeated actions, such as laughing, talking, or asking questions.

sentenceExamples.en: The neighbor's dog barked intensely all night long.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그는 자꾸 웃어 대서 분위기를 망쳤어요.
sentenceExamples.en: He kept laughing excessively and ruined the atmosphere.

sentenceExamples.kr: 전화가 계속 울려 대서 일을 못 하겠어요.
sentenceExamples.en: The phone keeps ringing so much I can't work.

name: -기가 무섭게
englishMeaning: As soon as / The moment that
briefDescription: Very immediate sequence. Similar to: -자마자 (No. 25).
featuredTranslation: The moment class ended, they rushed outside.
longerExplanation: This is a more emphatic version of '-자마자'. It emphasizes that there was absolutely no gap between the two actions. It translates literally to 'to the point where [X] is scary (fast).'

sentenceExamples.en: As soon as the sun set, the weather turned cold.

sentenceExamples.kr: 월급을 받기가 무섭게 다 써 버렸어요.
sentenceExamples.en: The moment I got my salary, I spent it all.
As soon as I open my eyes, I check my phone.

name: -아/어 내다
englishMeaning: To finish V-ing / Accomplish against odds
briefDescription: Achieving a difficult task. Similar to: -고 말다 (completion).
featuredTranslation: He finally pulled it off (accomplished it).
longerExplanation: This suffix is used when a result is achieved through the subject's persistence, willpower, or hard work. It's not just that the action finished, but that the subject *made* it finish despite difficulties.

sentenceExamples.en: I managed to solve the difficult problem.
He overcame (beat) the illness.
I will certainly find the culprit.

name: -(으)ㄴ/는 마당에
briefDescription: Setting a background situation (often negative). Similar to: -는데 (No. 97).
featuredExample: 모두가 돕는 마당에 너만 안 도와?
featuredTranslation: In a situation where everyone is helping, you're the only one not?
longerExplanation: Used to describe a background situation or context, often to point out a contradiction or to criticize someone's behavior given those circumstances. '마당' literally means 'yard' but here refers to the 'scene' or 'situation.'

sentenceExamples.kr: 헤어지는 마당에 무슨 말을 더 하겠어요?
sentenceExamples.en: Now that we're breaking up, what more is there to say?

sentenceExamples.kr: 경기가 안 좋은 마당에 창업은 위험해요.
sentenceExamples.en: Seeing as the economy is bad, starting a business is risky.

sentenceExamples.kr: 바쁜 마당에 한가하게 티비만 보고 있니?
sentenceExamples.en: Under these busy circumstances, are you just leisurely watching TV?

name: -다시피
briefDescription: Confirming shared knowledge or analogy. Similar to: -듯이 (No. 38).
featuredTranslation: As you know, I am a foreigner.
longerExplanation: Used in two ways: 1) With perception verbs (know, see, hear) to confirm something the listener already knows. 2) To mean 'almost the same as' (e.g., 'I lived at the library' - I didn't literally, but I was there so much it was like I did).

sentenceExamples.en: As you can see, the preparations are almost finished.
Because it's exam period, I practically live at the library.
As you've heard, that news is true.

name: -거들랑
briefDescription: Casual conditional. Similar to: -(으)면 (No. 106).
featuredTranslation: If (when) you get home, contact me.
longerExplanation: This is a colloquial form of '-(으)면'. It is mostly used in spoken language between close friends or to subordinates. It is often followed by a command or a suggestion.

sentenceExamples.en: If you have questions, ask me anytime.
If you're hungry, eat this.
If you meet him, say hello for me.

name: -(으)ㄹ 법하다
briefDescription: Logical probability. Similar to: -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 (No. 1).
featuredTranslation: That's a plausible (likely) story.
longerExplanation: Used when the speaker thinks a situation is logically reasonable or expected to happen. It's a stronger sense of 'it stands to reason' compared to a simple guess.

sentenceExamples.en: It's quite possible to make a mistake at least once.
It's understandable (likely) that he would be angry.
It was an accident that was quite likely to happen.

name: -고서
briefDescription: Action sequence emphasizing the first step. Similar to: -고 나서 (No. 96).
featuredTranslation: He laughed and then walked out.
longerExplanation: Used to connect two actions where the first action is a necessary preceding state or action for the second. It feels slightly more literary or descriptive than the simple '-고'.

sentenceExamples.en: Only after finishing the homework did I sleep.
Having heard that news, I was truly happy.
I'll decide after seeing it myself.

name: -기까지 하다
englishMeaning: Even goes as far as to V
briefDescription: Addition of an extreme characteristic. Similar to: -(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 (No. 30).
featuredTranslation: He is kind, and on top of that, he is even handsome.
longerExplanation: Used to emphasize an additional quality that goes beyond what is expected. It's like saying 'he is [X], and he is even [Y]!'. It adds an 'extra' level to the description.

sentenceExamples.kr: 비가 오는 데다가 바람이 불기까지 합니다.
sentenceExamples.en: It's raining, and what's more, it's even windy.
They have a good personality and are even smart too.
That restaurant was untasty and even unkind.

name: -(으)리라고
briefDescription: Formal/Literary prediction. Similar to: -(으)ㄹ 것이라고.
featuredTranslation: I believe that he will soon succeed.
longerExplanation: This is a formal and often poetic way to express a future conjecture or belief. It is frequently used with verbs like '믿다' (believe) or '생각하다' (think) in written texts or formal speeches.

sentenceExamples.en: It is expected that the weather will be good tomorrow.
I see it as likely that this matter will be resolved well.
I didn't even imagine that she would come.

name: -는 한
briefDescription: A condition that must persist for the result to hold. Similar to: -(으)면 (No. 106).
featuredExample: 내가 살아 있는 한 너를 지켜 줄게.
featuredTranslation: As long as I am alive, I will protect you.
longerExplanation: Used to set a boundary or condition of time or state. Action B remains true only as long as the state in Action A continues to exist.

sentenceExamples.en: Unless (as long as) something special doesn't happen, I will attend.
As long as you make an effort, nothing is impossible.
As long as you keep the rules, freedom is guaranteed.

name: -(으)ㄴ/는 모양이다
briefDescription: Conjecture based on objective evidence. Similar to: -나 보다 (No. 15).
featuredExample: 다들 우산을 쓰고 있는 걸 보니 비가 오는 모양이에요.
featuredTranslation: Seeing as everyone is using umbrellas, it appears to be raining.
longerExplanation: Used when the speaker makes a guess based on a factual, observed situation. It is more grounded in evidence than a simple '-것 같다'. '모양' literally means 'shape' or 'appearance.'

sentenceExamples.kr: 불이 꺼져 있는 걸 보니 벌써 자는 모양이에요.
sentenceExamples.en: Since the lights are off, it appears they are already sleeping.

sentenceExamples.kr: 표정이 안 좋은 걸 보니 무슨 일이 있는 모양이에요.
sentenceExamples.en: Given their expression, it looks like something is wrong.

sentenceExamples.kr: 가방이 없는 걸 보니 벌써 나간 모양입니다.
sentenceExamples.en: Since their bag is gone, it appears they've already left.

name: -다면서요?
englishMeaning: Is it true that...? / I heard that...
briefDescription: Confirming information heard from others. Similar to: -다던데 (No. 56).
featuredTranslation: I heard you're getting married next month, is that right?
longerExplanation: Used when the speaker wants to confirm something they heard previously. It can express surprise or just a desire for clarification. It's a combination of '-다고 하다' (say) and '-면서' (while).

sentenceExamples.en: I heard you like Korean food, right?
I heard you passed the exam; congratulations!
I heard you were very sick yesterday; are you okay now?

name: -다니(까)
englishMeaning: I told you that... / Since I said...
briefDescription: Emphasizing or repeating a previous statement. Similar to: -라고 하다 (No. 199).
featuredTranslation: I'm telling you, it's true!
longerExplanation: Used when the speaker wants to emphasize a point they already made, often because the listener didn't seem to believe them or act on it. It adds a bit of assertive force to the reason.

sentenceExamples.en: I told you to wait a bit, so why do you keep asking?
I told you it's dangerous there, so don't go.
I'm telling you, I did it all.

name: -(으)ㄹ 줄 알았다/몰랐다
briefDescription: Expressing a past assumption or realization. Similar to: -는 줄 몰랐다 (No. 51).
featuredTranslation: I knew (thought) it would rain.
longerExplanation: '-알았다' means the speaker's assumption was correct or that they held a belief that turned out to be true/false. '-몰랐다' means they were completely unaware or surprised by a fact they hadn't considered.

sentenceExamples.en: I thought you weren't Korean (but you are).
I didn't know today was your birthday; I'm sorry.
I didn't know it would be this difficult.

name: -다가는
briefDescription: Warning about a negative consequence. Similar to: -(으)면 (No. 106).
featuredTranslation: If you keep playing like that, you'll fail the exam.
longerExplanation: Specifically used for warnings. It implies that a current continuous action will lead to a disaster or negative outcome if it doesn't stop. It projects a negative future based on current behavior.

sentenceExamples.kr: 매일 술을 마시다가는 건강을 해칠 거예요.
sentenceExamples.en: If you keep drinking every day, you'll ruin your health.
If you start without preparation, it's easy to fail.
If you keep lying, you will lose trust.

name: -기는커녕
briefDescription: Strongly denying the first clause. Similar to: -은커녕 (No. 36).
featuredTranslation: Far from being praised, I only got scolded.
longerExplanation: Used to emphasize that not only is the expected result impossible, but even a basic/lower level of that result is out of the question. It highlights a much worse reality than what was hoped for.

sentenceExamples.en: Far from winning the prize money, I just wasted the entry fee.
Far from the work decreasing, it has become even more.
Far from hearing thanks, I was criticized.

name: -다더니
englishMeaning: I heard (you said) X, and now Y
briefDescription: Recalling a past statement and contrasting it with the current situation. Similar to: -더니 (No. 68).
featuredTranslation: You said you were on a diet, but you're eating pizza?
longerExplanation: Used when you recall someone (or yourself) saying something in the past, and you are now pointing out the result or the contradiction to that statement.

sentenceExamples.en: He said he was going to study, but he's just playing games.
You said you'd come early, so why did you just arrive now?
You said it wasn't spicy, but it's too spicy.

name: -다니까
briefDescription: Giving a reason based on a stated fact or command. Similar to: -다니 (No. 153).
featuredTranslation: Since they said it's raining tomorrow, let's stay home.
longerExplanation: Used when a previous statement or a widely known fact becomes the basis for the suggestion or decision in the following clause. It's common in making group plans.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 식당이 맛있다니까 한번 가 봐요.
sentenceExamples.en: Since they say that restaurant is good, let's try going there.
Since they said the teacher is waiting, let's go quickly.
Since they say there's a sale, shall we go to the department store?

name: -고 말다
briefDescription: Indicates an action that was finally completed, often with a nuance of regret. Similar to: -아/어 버리다 (No. 17).
featuredTranslation: I worked hard but ended up failing.
longerExplanation: Unlike '-아/어 버리다' which can show relief, '-고 말다' usually implies that the result was unintended, disappointing, or the final outcome after a long struggle. It is often used in news and formal writing.

sentenceExamples.en: I tried to hold it in but ended up crying.
An accident ended up happening.
After long effort, we finally (and surely) achieved victory.

name: -자니
englishMeaning: Now that I think of V-ing... / Since I intend to...
briefDescription: Expressing hesitation or a reason based on a potential action. Similar to: -(으)려니까.
featuredTranslation: Now that I'm thinking of going alone, it's a bit scary.
longerExplanation: Used when the speaker considers doing something, but that specific thought leads to a concern, a feeling, or a reason for another action. It often contrasts two options (Going is X, staying is Y).

sentenceExamples.en: Buying it is expensive, but not buying it is a pity.
Asking is embarrassing, but not asking is frustrating.
Since I'm thinking of throwing it away, it feels like a waste so I can't.

name: -(으)ㄴ 끝에
englishMeaning: After a long period of... / At the end of...
briefDescription: Indicates a result achieved after a prolonged process or struggle. Similar to: -고 나서 (No. 96).
featuredTranslation: After long agonizing, I submitted my resignation.
longerExplanation: This emphasizes the effort and the long duration of time leading up to the final result. It's usually used with nouns or verbs describing hardship, deep thought, or intense struggle.

sentenceExamples.en: After long effort, they succeeded.
At the end of the meeting, they reached an agreement.
After the surgery (the long process), they recovered their health.

name: -아/어 내다
englishMeaning: To finish V-ing / Accomplish against the odds
briefDescription: Successfully achieving a difficult task through willpower. Similar to: -고 말다 (No. 159).
featuredTranslation: He finally pulled it off (accomplished it).
longerExplanation: This suffix is added to a verb when a result is achieved specifically because of the subject's persistence or hard work. It carries a positive nuance of 'overcoming' something.

sentenceExamples.en: I managed to solve the difficult problem.
He overcame (beat) the illness.
I will certainly find the culprit.

name: -아/어 대다
briefDescription: Repetition of an action, usually with a negative or bothersome nuance. Similar to: -곤 하다 (No. 79).
featuredTranslation: I had a hard time because the child kept crying (intensely).
longerExplanation: Used when an action is repeated over and over in an excessive or irritating way. It often expresses the speaker's frustration with someone else's behavior.

sentenceExamples.en: The neighbor's dog barked intensely all night long.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그는 자꾸 웃어 대서 분위기를 망쳤어요.
sentenceExamples.en: He kept laughing excessively and ruined the atmosphere.

sentenceExamples.kr: 전화가 계속 울려 대서 일을 못 하겠어요.
sentenceExamples.en: The phone keeps ringing so much I can't work.

name: -기가 무섭게
englishMeaning: As soon as / The moment that (Very fast)
briefDescription: Very immediate sequence between two actions. Similar to: -자마자 (No. 25).
featuredTranslation: The moment class ended, they rushed outside.
longerExplanation: This is a more emphatic and dramatic version of '-자마자'. It suggests that the second action happened with 'scary' speed as soon as the first one finished.

sentenceExamples.en: As soon as the sun set, the weather turned cold.

sentenceExamples.kr: 월급을 받기가 무섭게 다 써 버렸어요.
sentenceExamples.en: The moment I got my salary, I spent it all.
As soon as I open my eyes, I check my phone.

name: -다시피
briefDescription: Confirming shared knowledge or using an analogy. Similar to: -듯이 (No. 38).
featuredTranslation: As you know, I am a foreigner.
longerExplanation: Commonly used with perception verbs (know, see, hear) to reference information the listener is already aware of. It can also mean 'almost as if' for exaggeration.

sentenceExamples.en: As you can see, the preparations are almost finished.
Because it's exam period, I practically live at the library.
As you've heard, that news is true.

name: -(으)ㄴ/는 마당에
briefDescription: Setting a background context, often with a nuance of irony or criticism. Similar to: -는데 (No. 97).
featuredExample: 모두가 돕는 마당에 너만 안 도와?
featuredTranslation: In a situation where everyone is helping, you're the only one not?
longerExplanation: Used to describe a background situation, usually to point out a contradiction or to criticize someone's behavior given the current state of things. '마당' refers to the 'scene.'

sentenceExamples.kr: 헤어지는 마당에 무슨 말을 더 하겠어요?
sentenceExamples.en: Now that we're breaking up, what more is there to say?

sentenceExamples.kr: 경기가 안 좋은 마당에 창업은 위험해요.
sentenceExamples.en: Seeing as the economy is bad, starting a business is risky.

sentenceExamples.kr: 바쁜 마당에 한가하게 티비만 보고 있니?
sentenceExamples.en: In this busy situation, are you just leisurely watching TV?

name: -(으)ㄹ 법하다
briefDescription: Logical probability or reasonable expectation. Similar to: -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 (No. 1).
featuredTranslation: That's a plausible (likely) story.
longerExplanation: Used when the speaker believes a situation is logically reasonable or expected to happen. It feels more 'objective' than a simple guess.

sentenceExamples.en: It's quite possible to make a mistake at least once.
It's understandable (likely) that he would be angry.
It was an accident that was quite likely to happen.

name: -거들랑
briefDescription: Casual conditional mostly used in speaking. Similar to: -(으)면 (No. 106).
featuredTranslation: If (when) you get home, contact me.
longerExplanation: A colloquial form of '-(으)면'. It is mostly used between close friends or to subordinates, usually followed by a command, request, or suggestion.

sentenceExamples.en: If you have questions, ask me anytime.
If you're hungry, eat this.
If you meet him, say hello for me.

name: -(으)ㄹ 따름이다
briefDescription: Expressing a humble or limited state. Similar to: -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 (No. 53).
featuredTranslation: I am merely happy that I can help.
longerExplanation: A formal and literary version of '-(으)ㄹ 뿐이다'. It is often used to express a strong, singular emotion like being sorry, grateful, or surprised without any other thoughts.

sentenceExamples.en: I am just (merely) sorry.
I was nothing but surprised to hear that news.
I merely did the work I was assigned.

name: -(으)ㄹ 뿐더러
briefDescription: Adding more information. Similar to: -(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 (No. 30).
featuredTranslation: He is not only smart but also humble.
longerExplanation: More formal and literary than '-(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라'. It is frequently used in written TOPIK texts and news to connect two complementary qualities.

sentenceExamples.kr: 날씨가 쌀쌀할 뿐더러 바람도 많이 불어요.
sentenceExamples.en: The weather is not only chilly but also windy.

sentenceExamples.kr: 이 식당은 맛있을 뿐더러 가격도 싸요.
sentenceExamples.en: This restaurant is not only tasty but also cheap.
That movie was not only interesting but also touching.

name: -(으)ㄹ락 말락 하다
englishMeaning: On the verge of / Flickering between
briefDescription: Indicates an action is about to happen but hasn't quite happened yet.
featuredTranslation: I'm just about to fall asleep (drifting in and out).
longerExplanation: Used when something is right on the edge of happening. It implies a repeating motion of almost starting and then stopping.

sentenceExamples.en: It looks like it's going to rain any second (but isn't quite yet).
The memory is right on the tip of my tongue.
An island that is barely visible on the horizon.

name: -(으)ㄴ/는 셈 치다
englishMeaning: Consider it as / Act as if
briefDescription: Acting as if a situation is different from reality. Similar to: -는 셈이다 (No. 5).
featuredExample: 속는 셈 치고 한번 믿어 보세요.
featuredTranslation: Just trust me once, even if you feel like you're being tricked.
longerExplanation: Used when the speaker decides to treat a situation as a certain way for the sake of mindset, even if the actual facts are different. 'Let's just say...' is the English equivalent.

sentenceExamples.kr: 여행 갔다 온 셈 치고 그 돈을 저금했어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I acted as if I had gone on a trip and saved that money instead.
Let's just act as if we forgot it and start anew.
I'll consider it as a gift.

name: -(으)ㄹ 겸 (해서)
englishMeaning: To do V and also (dual purpose)
briefDescription: Indicating that an action has two or more purposes. Similar to: -기 위해서 (No. 32).
featuredTranslation: I went to the park to take a walk and also (for other reasons).
longerExplanation: Used when you perform one action to satisfy multiple goals. Often used as 'A도 할 겸 B도 할 겸'.

sentenceExamples.en: I went on a trip to get some fresh air and also (for a break).

sentenceExamples.kr: 돈도 벌 겸 경험도 쌓을 겸 아르바이트를 해요.
sentenceExamples.en: I do a part-time job to both earn money and gain experience.
I went downtown to meet a friend and also (do some errands).

name: -(으)ㄴ/는 김에
englishMeaning: While one is at it / Since you're already...
briefDescription: Using an existing opportunity to do another related action. Similar to: -는 길에 (No. 29).
featuredExample: 마트에 가는 김에 우유 좀 사다 주세요.
featuredTranslation: While you are going to the mart, please buy some milk too.
longerExplanation: This is about efficiency. Since you are already performing Action A, you decide to perform Action B as well because it's convenient or related.

sentenceExamples.en: Since I was already downtown, I stopped by the bookstore too.

sentenceExamples.kr: 일어난 김에 물 한 잔만 주세요.
sentenceExamples.en: Since you're already up, please give me a glass of water.
Since I started cleaning anyway, I wiped the windows too.

name: -(으)ㄹ 테니까
briefDescription: Giving a reason based on intent or a strong prediction. Similar to: -(으)니까 (No. 105).
featuredTranslation: Since I will do the cleaning, you do the cooking.
longerExplanation: Two uses: 1) First person intent: 'I'll do this, so you do that.' 2) Third person prediction: 'It will likely be like this, so you should do that.'

sentenceExamples.en: Since it will likely be cold outside, dress warmly.
Since I'm buying, please eat as much as you like.

sentenceExamples.kr: 곧 도착할 테니까 조금만 기다려 줘.
sentenceExamples.en: Since I'll arrive soon, please wait just a little bit.

name: -(으)ㄹ 테지만
briefDescription: Contrasting a strong prediction with another fact. Similar to: -(으)ㄹ 텐데 (No. 76).
featuredTranslation: I imagine you'll be busy, but please come anyway.
longerExplanation: Combines a strong guess/prediction ('-을 테-') with contrast ('-지만'). It acknowledges an expected situation before introducing a counter-request or fact.

sentenceExamples.en: I imagine it will be hard, but please endure it for a bit.
It will likely be expensive, but the quality will be good.

sentenceExamples.kr: 피곤할 테지만 숙제는 다 해야 해요.
sentenceExamples.en: You must be tired, but you have to finish all your homework.

name: -(으)ㄹ지도 모르다
englishMeaning: Might / May / Might not know if...
briefDescription: Expressing a slight possibility or uncertainty. Similar to: -(으)ㄹ 수도 있다.
featuredTranslation: It might rain tomorrow.
longerExplanation: Used for low-probability events or when the speaker is not at all sure. It's like saying 'I don't know, it's a possibility.'

sentenceExamples.en: He might have left already.
The roads might be blocked, so let's head out early.
The exam might be harder than you think.

name: V-다 보면
briefDescription: Predicting a result if an action is continuously repeated. Similar to: -다 보니까 (No. 37).
featuredExample: 열심히 공부하다 보면 실력이 늘 거예요.
featuredTranslation: If you keep studying hard, your skills will naturally improve.
longerExplanation: Combines '-다가' (ongoing action) with '-면' (if). It focuses on the natural result that will occur in the future if the current behavior continues.

sentenceExamples.en: If you keep practicing, you'll get used to it.

sentenceExamples.kr: 살다 보면 이런 일도 있고 저런 일도 있어요.
sentenceExamples.en: If you live long enough, things like this and that happen.
If you keep walking, you'll see the destination.

name: V-다 보니까
englishMeaning: While doing V / Since I was doing V (Realization)
briefDescription: Discovering a fact or achieving a state while performing an action. Similar to: -다 보니.
featuredExample: 이야기를 하다 보니까 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어요.
featuredTranslation: While talking, I didn't realize time was passing.
longerExplanation: Similar to No. 178, but '-다 보니까' is used for actions that have already happened or are happening, leading to a past realization or a current state.

sentenceExamples.kr: 한국 음식을 먹다 보니까 이제 매운 것도 잘 먹어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Since I've been eating Korean food, I can now eat spicy things well.
While living busily, I ended up losing my health.

sentenceExamples.kr: 혼자 살다 보니까 요리를 잘하게 됐어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Since I live alone, I've become good at cooking.

name: V-(으)ㄴ 지 N(시간)이 되다
briefDescription: Expressing the duration of time since an action occurred.
featuredTranslation: It has been one year since I came to Korea.
longerExplanation: The action in the first clause is finished, and the second part specifies the interval of time that has passed since then. Always used with the past noun form '-(으)ㄴ'.

sentenceExamples.en: It's been over 6 months since I quit smoking.
It's been a long time since I last saw him.

sentenceExamples.kr: 밥을 먹은 지 얼마 안 됐어요.
sentenceExamples.en: It hasn't been long since I ate.

name: 하도 A/V-아서/어서
briefDescription: Used when an extreme degree of a state or action is the reason for a result. Similar to: -아/어서 (No. 102).
featuredTranslation: I was so tired that I fell asleep without even washing up.
longerExplanation: Adding '하도' before the reason structure '-아서/어서' emphasizes that the cause was excessive or extreme. It is often used when complaining or explaining an unusual outcome caused by that intensity.

sentenceExamples.en: I was so hungry that I ate ravenously.

sentenceExamples.kr: 아이들이 하도 떠드는 통에 정신이 없었어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Because the kids were making such a racket, I couldn't think straight.
The roads were so blocked that I was late for my appointment.

name: A/V-았던/었던
briefDescription: Recalls a past state or action that is finished and no longer continues. Similar to: -던 (No. 192).
featuredTranslation: This is the house where I used to live (but don't anymore).
longerExplanation: This retrospective suffix emphasizes that the past event is completely disconnected from the present. It often contrasts the past state with the current state.

sentenceExamples.en: I finished reading the book I was reading yesterday.

sentenceExamples.kr: 작년에 갔던 해수욕장에 다시 가고 싶어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I want to go back to the beach I went to last year.

sentenceExamples.kr: 날씨가 맑았던 아침과 달리 지금은 비가 와요.
sentenceExamples.en: Unlike this morning when it was clear, it's raining now.

name: A-아/어하다
englishMeaning: To feel/appear to be (Adjective to Verb)
briefDescription: Turns an adjective into a verb to describe a third person's feelings or state. Similar to: -아/어 보이다 (No. 77).
featuredTranslation: My younger sibling is happy after receiving the gift.
longerExplanation: In Korean, many emotional adjectives (like 슬프다, 기쁘다) can only be used by the first person. To describe how someone else feels based on their behavior, you must add '-아/어하다'.

sentenceExamples.kr: 부모님께서 제 합격 소식을 듣고 좋아하셨어요.
sentenceExamples.en: My parents were happy to hear the news of my passing.
The child is afraid of the dog.
The students are curious about the exam results.

name: A/V-(으)ㄹ걸(요)
briefDescription: Used to express a conjecture or disagreement with the listener. Similar to: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (No. 20).
featuredTranslation: I bet it will probably rain tomorrow.
longerExplanation: This is a conversational ending used when the speaker is guessing about a future event or a fact they aren't 100% sure of. It often carries a slight nuance of 'I think so (contrary to what you might think)'.

sentenceExamples.en: I suspect that person has already left work.
I bet the roads will be very crowded if you go now.
I bet that movie isn't very interesting.

name: A/V-지 않으면 안 되다
briefDescription: Emphasizes obligation using a double negative. Similar to: -아야/어야 하다 (No. 110).
featuredExample: 이 서류는 오늘까지 제출하지 않으면 안 돼요.
featuredTranslation: You absolutely must submit this document by today.
longerExplanation: Literally 'If you don't do [X], it doesn't work.' It is a more emphatic and formal way to express necessity compared to the standard '-아야 하다'.

sentenceExamples.kr: 건강을 위해서 운동을 하지 않으면 안 됩니다.
sentenceExamples.en: You must exercise for your health.

sentenceExamples.kr: 한국에서 살려면 한국어를 배우지 않으면 안 돼요.
sentenceExamples.en: If you intend to live in Korea, you must learn Korean.

sentenceExamples.kr: 약속 시간을 지키지 않으면 안 돼요.
sentenceExamples.en: You absolutely must keep the appointment time.

name: N만 하다
briefDescription: Used to compare the size, amount, or degree of something to a noun. Similar to: N만큼 (No. 100 similar).
featuredTranslation: My bag is about the size of this apple.
longerExplanation: This is used for comparisons of scale. It is often used to describe how large or small something is by referencing a familiar object.

sentenceExamples.en: My salary is as small as a rat's tail (tiny).

sentenceExamples.kr: 목소리가 모기만 해서 잘 안 들려요.
sentenceExamples.en: Your voice is as small as a mosquito's, so I can't hear you well.
The house is as big as a palace.

name: V-(으)ㄹ 생각도 못 하다
englishMeaning: Can't even think of doing V
briefDescription: Indicates that something is so difficult or overwhelming that one cannot even imagine doing it.
featuredExample: 너무 비싸서 살 생각도 못 했어요.
featuredTranslation: It was so expensive I couldn't even think of buying it.
longerExplanation: This expression highlights an extreme limitation, usually due to lack of money, time, or ability. It goes beyond just 'I can't do it' to 'it never even entered my mind as a possibility'.

sentenceExamples.kr: 일이 많아서 쉴 생각도 못 해요.
sentenceExamples.en: I have so much work I can't even dream of resting.

sentenceExamples.kr: 너무 긴장해서 대답할 생각도 못 했어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I was so nervous I couldn't even think of answering.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그때는 너무 어려서 유학 갈 생각도 못 했지요.
sentenceExamples.en: I was so young then that I couldn't even imagine studying abroad.

name: A/V-기로 유명하다
briefDescription: Used to state why a person, place, or thing is well-known. Similar to: N(으)로 유명하다.
featuredTranslation: This restaurant is famous for its delicious bibimbap.
longerExplanation: Attaches to the nominalized verb form '-기'. It is used to provide the specific reason or characteristic for which something has a widespread reputation.

sentenceExamples.en: That actor is famous for their good acting.
Korea is famous for its fast internet speed.
Jeju is an island famous for being very windy.

name: A/V-다니(요)? / N-(이)라니(요)?
briefDescription: Used to express surprise, disbelief, or shock at something the listener said.
featuredTranslation: I can't believe that person is already married!
longerExplanation: This ending repeats what the other person said back to them as a question of disbelief. It is short for '-다고 하니(요)'. It effectively communicates 'Really? Is that true?'.

sentenceExamples.en: Tomorrow is the exam? You can't be serious! I didn't know.
I can't believe it's this expensive! That's too much.
I can't believe a foreigner speaks Korean this well!

name: N(이)라고 (해서) 다 ... 것은 아니다
englishMeaning: Just because N, it doesn't mean all...
briefDescription: Used for partial negation, showing that a general rule doesn't apply to every case.
featuredExample: 한국 사람이라고 해서 다 김치를 좋아하는 것은 아니에요.
featuredTranslation: Just because someone is Korean, it doesn't mean they all like kimchi.
longerExplanation: This is a logical structure used to challenge stereotypes or generalizations. It admits the first fact (the person is Korean) but denies that the expected result (liking kimchi) is universally true.

sentenceExamples.kr: 돈이 많다고 해서 다 행복한 것은 아닙니다.
sentenceExamples.en: Just because you have a lot of money, it doesn't mean you are always happy.

sentenceExamples.kr: 학생이라고 해서 다 공부를 열심히 하는 것은 아니에요.
sentenceExamples.en: Just because they are students, it doesn't mean everyone studies hard.

sentenceExamples.kr: 비싸다고 해서 다 품질이 좋은 것은 아니에요.
sentenceExamples.en: Just because it's expensive, it doesn't mean the quality is always good.

name: V-고 말다
englishMeaning: Ended up V-ing / Finally did V
briefDescription: Indicates an action that happened unintentionally or was finally achieved after difficulty. Similar to: -아/어 버리다 (No. 17).
featuredTranslation: I tried to hold it in, but I ended up laughing.
longerExplanation: 1) Unintentional: Something happened against your will. 2) Determination/Completion: Finally achieving a goal after a long process. Unlike '-아/어 버리다', it is more often used in formal writing or news.

sentenceExamples.kr: 밤을 새워 공부했지만 시험에서 실수하고 말았어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I stayed up all night studying but ended up making a mistake on the exam.
We finally (and surely) achieved victory.
I ended up missing the train.

name: A/V-던
briefDescription: Used to recall a past habit or an action that was not finished. Similar to: -았던/었던 (No. 182).
featuredExample: 이 노래는 제가 자주 듣던 노래예요.
featuredTranslation: This is a song I used to listen to often.
longerExplanation: '-던' implies that the past action was either a regular habit or something that was in progress but interrupted. Unlike '-았던/었던', it doesn't necessarily mean the state is completely disconnected from now; it just 'looks back' at the scene.

sentenceExamples.kr: 어제 마시다 던 커피가 책상 위에 있어요.
sentenceExamples.en: The coffee I was drinking yesterday (unfinished) is on the desk.
This is the elementary school I used to attend.
Please continue the story you were telling earlier.

name: A/V-잖아(요)
englishMeaning: As you know / You know that...
briefDescription: Used to remind the listener of a fact they should already know or to confirm shared information.
featuredTranslation: You know we agreed to meet tomorrow (right?).
longerExplanation: This is a very common conversational ending. It can be used to give a reason, to scold someone lightly, or simply to confirm agreement. It translates roughly to 'Don't you remember?' or 'Isn't it because...?'

sentenceExamples.en: Today is a holiday, you know. We should rest.
I told you earlier (remember?).
It's not hard, right? Give it a try.

name: V-(으)려면 멀었다
englishMeaning: A long way to go before...
briefDescription: Indicates that much more time or effort is needed to reach a certain goal or state.
featuredTranslation: I still have a long way to go before my Korean skills improve.
longerExplanation: Used to express humility or to state that a plan is far from completion. '멀다' means 'far', so literally 'to [V], it is still far'.

sentenceExamples.kr: 밥을 다 먹으려면 멀었으니까 먼저 가세요.
sentenceExamples.en: It'll be a long while before I finish eating, so please go ahead.
We are still a long way from reaching home.
I have a long way to go to become an expert.

name: 얼마나 A-(으)ㄴ지 / V-는지 모르다
briefDescription: Used to emphasize the high degree of a state or action. Similar to: 아주, 매우 (Very).
featuredTranslation: You have no idea how sad that movie is! (It's extremely sad).
longerExplanation: This is a rhetorical structure. It literally means 'I don't know how [X] it is', but it functions as a strong exclamation. It is very common in spoken Korean to add flavor and emphasis.

sentenceExamples.en: You don't know how busy I've been lately!

sentenceExamples.kr: 제 친구가 얼마나 노래를 잘하는지 몰라요.
sentenceExamples.en: My friend sings so incredibly well.
You have no idea how spicy Korean food can be.

name: A-다고 하다 / V-ㄴ다고 하다
briefDescription: The basic form for reporting what someone else said. Similar to: -대요 (No. 198).
featuredTranslation: My friend said it will rain tomorrow.
longerExplanation: This is the most fundamental indirect quotation structure. It changes depending on the word class: Adjectives use '-다고', Verbs use '-ㄴ/는다고', and Nouns use '-(이)라고'.

sentenceExamples.kr: 선생님이 이 책이 아주 좋다고 하셨어요.
sentenceExamples.en: The teacher said this book is very good.
Sumi says she is studying now.
That person said they are a student.

name: V-아야겠다 / 어야겠다
briefDescription: Expresses a strong personal resolution or a realization that an action is necessary. Similar to: -(으)려고 하다 (No. 85).
featuredTranslation: I'm so tired, I really should get some rest.
longerExplanation: This structure is used when the speaker makes a decision based on the current situation. It feels more like a spontaneous realization of necessity than a long-term planned intention.

sentenceExamples.en: I'm hungry, so I should eat first.
It's raining. I must take an umbrella.
I should go home now. It's too late.

name: A/V-대(요) / N-(이)래(요)
briefDescription: The casual/spoken version of reported speech. Similar to: -다고 하다 (No. 196).
featuredTranslation: I heard that movie is really fun.
longerExplanation: This is a contraction of '-다고 해요'. It is the most common way to relay rumors or information you heard from others in daily conversation.

sentenceExamples.en: I heard Minsu is busy right now.
They say it's going to snow this evening.
I heard that person is a student at our school.

name: V-(으)라고 하다
briefDescription: Used to report a command or request made by someone else.
featuredTranslation: My mom told me to come home early.
longerExplanation: Used when reporting an imperative sentence. If the original command ended in '-(으)세요' or '-(으)라', it is reported as '-(으)라고 하다'.

sentenceExamples.en: The doctor told me to quit drinking.

sentenceExamples.kr: 친구가 내일 6시에 만나자고... 아니, 만나라고 했어요.
sentenceExamples.en: My friend told me to meet (him) at 6 tomorrow.
The teacher tells us to make sure to do the homework.

name: 누구나, 언제나, 어디나
briefDescription: Combinations of question words and '나' to express 'any/every' without exception.
featuredTranslation: There are many people everywhere.
longerExplanation: By adding the particle '나' to question words (누구, 언제, 어디, 무엇, 어느), you create universal pronouns. Note that they can also mean 'anyone/anytime' depending on context.

sentenceExamples.en: Anyone can make a mistake.
I am always rooting for you.
Anything is all fine.

name: A/V-(으)냐고 하다[묻다]
briefDescription: Used to report a question asked by someone else.
featuredTranslation: My friend asked if I have time this weekend.
longerExplanation: When reporting a question, the suffix changes to '-(으)냐고'. In spoken Korean, this is often shortened to '-냬요'. It is typically followed by verbs like '하다' or '묻다' (to ask).

sentenceExamples.en: The teacher asked if I finished the homework.
Don't ask me where I'm going.
I asked the clerk how much this is.

name: A/V-던데(요)
briefDescription: Used to provide background information or context based on the speaker's past observation. Similar to: -더라고요 (No. 55).
featuredExample: 어제 가 보니까 백화점에 사람이 많던데요.
featuredTranslation: (I saw that) there were many people at the department store yesterday.
longerExplanation: This ending is used when the speaker recalls a past scene and uses it to suggest something or to express a mild surprise. It often functions as a 'hook' for the next sentence.

sentenceExamples.en: I found the food at that restaurant to be delicious.
I saw it was raining earlier, so take an umbrella.
I saw (experienced) that Minsu sings really well.

name: V-(으)ㄹ까 말까 (하다)
briefDescription: Expresses indecision or hesitation between performing an action or not.
featuredExample: 그 옷을 살까 말까 고민 중이에요.
featuredTranslation: I'm worried about whether to buy those clothes or not.
longerExplanation: This is a common way to express that you are 'on the fence' about a decision. It literally means 'Should I do it? Should I not?'

sentenceExamples.kr: 비가 와서 나갈까 말까 하고 있어요.
sentenceExamples.en: It's raining, so I'm debating whether to go out or not.
I'm hesitating about whether to confess my feelings or not.
I'm thinking about whether or not to go on a trip this weekend.

name: V-지 그래요?
briefDescription: A polite way to make a suggestion or give advice to someone. Similar to: -(으)세요 (No. 116 similar).
featuredTranslation: If you're tired, why don't you rest a bit?
longerExplanation: Literally 'Why don't you do [X]?'. It is used when the speaker believes the suggested action is the best course of action for the listener. It is polite but carries a definite recommendation.

sentenceExamples.en: If you don't know, why don't you ask the teacher?

sentenceExamples.kr: 혼자 힘들면 친구에게 도와달라고 하지 그래요?
sentenceExamples.en: If it's hard alone, why don't you ask a friend for help?

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 옷이 마음에 들면 사지 그래요?
sentenceExamples.en: If you like those clothes, why don't you buy them?

name: V-(으)ㄹ걸 (그랬다)
briefDescription: Expresses regret about a past action that was not taken. Similar to: -았어야 했는데 (No. 54).
featuredTranslation: I should have gone to bed early yesterday (I regret not doing so).
longerExplanation: This is a conversational way to express 'If only I had done [X]'. It is always used for things that didn't happen but the speaker wishes had happened.

sentenceExamples.en: I should have brought an umbrella.
I should have told the truth back then.

sentenceExamples.kr: 밥을 좀 더 먹을걸 그랬나 봐요.
sentenceExamples.en: I guess I should have eaten a bit more.

name: N(이)라도
englishMeaning: Even if it's just... / At least...
briefDescription: Used to suggest a second-best option when the ideal one is unavailable.
featuredTranslation: If there's no coffee, please give me at least some tea.
longerExplanation: '-라도' implies that while the chosen noun isn't the best, it is acceptable or sufficient under the circumstances. It can also be used for emphasis (e.g., 'even a child knows').

sentenceExamples.en: If you're bored, at least read a comic book.
I want to rest even if it's just for 5 minutes.
Should I (at least) help you?

name: A/V-거든(요)
briefDescription: Used to provide a reason or background that the listener doesn't know. Similar to: -기 때문이에요 (No. 111).
featuredTranslation: The thing is, I'm a bit busy right now.
longerExplanation: This ending is used when the speaker is explaining something or giving a reason for their behavior. It has a slightly defensive or clarifying nuance, often used when responding to a question or a look of confusion.

sentenceExamples.kr: 어제 잠을 못 잤거든요. 그래서 피곤해요.
sentenceExamples.en: You see, I couldn't sleep yesterday. That's why I'm tired.
The thing is, this restaurant is really famous.
It's because tomorrow is my friend's birthday.

name: 아무 N도
englishMeaning: No N at all / Not a single N
briefDescription: Used with negative endings to express absolute negation of a noun.
featuredTranslation: There is no one (here).
longerExplanation: Combining '아무' (any) with a noun and the particle '도' (even/also) creates a strong 'not any' meaning. It must be followed by a negative verb ending like '없다' or '안 하다'.

sentenceExamples.en: Don't say a single word.
There's not a single sound in the classroom.
There's nothing (not a thing) in my pocket.

name: V-이/히/리/기-
briefDescription: Suffixes added to verbs to turn them into the passive voice (the subject receives the action).
featuredTranslation: The thief was caught by the police.
longerExplanation: Korean uses specific suffixes to make verbs passive. The choice between '이, 히, 리, 기' depends on the specific verb root. For example: 보다 -> 보이다 (be seen), 닫다 -> 닫히다 (be closed), 듣다 -> 들리다 (be heard).

sentenceExamples.en: The window is closed.
The mountain is visible over there (is being seen).
A baby's crying can be heard.

name: V-았다가 / 었다가
englishMeaning: Did V and then shifted (State change)
briefDescription: Indicates that one action was completed, and then a reverse or different action occurred. Similar to: -다가 (No. 73).
featuredTranslation: I went to the convenience store and (on the way back/after) met a friend.
longerExplanation: Unlike '-다가' (which interrupts an action), '-았다가' implies the first action was fully finished before the second one started. It is often used for round trips or changes in state (e.g., 'turned it on and then off').

sentenceExamples.en: I turned the light on and then turned it off again.

sentenceExamples.kr: 가방을 샀다가 마음에 안 들어서 환불했어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I bought the bag but returned it because I didn't like it.
I went out but came back quickly because it rained.

name: A/V-아야 할 텐데(요)
briefDescription: Expresses the speaker's worry or hope that a certain condition will be met. Similar to: -(으)면 좋겠다 (No. 3).
featuredTranslation: I really hope the weather will be good tomorrow.
longerExplanation: This combines the obligation '-아야 하다' with the conjecture '-ㄹ 텐데'. It shows that the speaker is anxious about a situation and strongly desires a specific positive outcome.

sentenceExamples.en: I hope I won't be late; I'm worried.
I really ought to do well on the exam (I hope so).

sentenceExamples.kr: 빨리 도착해야 할 텐데 길이 너무 막히네요.
sentenceExamples.en: We really need to arrive quickly, but the road is so blocked.

name: A/V-는데도 불구하고
englishMeaning: In spite of... / Despite the fact that...
briefDescription: A stronger and more formal version of '-는데도'. Similar to: -는데도 (No. 41).
featuredTranslation: Despite the rain, they continued the match.
longerExplanation: This is a formal/literary structure. It emphasizes that the result happened even though there was a very strong reason for it not to. It is frequently used in news and academic writing.

sentenceExamples.en: Despite being sick, they went to work.
In spite of the difficult situation, they succeeded.
Despite the hard effort, they ended up failing.

name: N에 대해(서) / N에 대한 N
briefDescription: Used to indicate the topic or subject of an action or thought.
featuredTranslation: I want to learn about Korean culture.
longerExplanation: When followed by a verb, use 'N에 대해서'. When modifying a noun directly, use 'N에 대한 N' (e.g., 'a book about culture' -> 문화에 대한 책). It is the standard way to introduce a topic of discussion.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 문제에 대해 더 이야기해 봅시다.
sentenceExamples.en: Let's talk more about that problem.
I have many worries about the future.
A seminar about environmental pollution was held.

name: 어찌나 A/V-(으)ㄴ/는지
englishMeaning: So... that... / To such an extent
briefDescription: Used to emphasize the extreme degree of a state or action. Similar to: 얼마나 -는지 모르다 (No. 195).
featuredTranslation: I was so hungry that I ate three portions by myself.
longerExplanation: This structure is used to highlight an excessive situation that leads to a specific result. It is more emphatic than a simple '-아서/어서' and often pairs with '-는지 모르다' or a result clause showing surprise.

sentenceExamples.kr: 어찌나 피곤한지 세수도 못 하고 잤어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I was so tired that I fell asleep without even washing my face.

sentenceExamples.kr: 어찌나 공부를 열심히 하는지 항상 1등을 해요.
sentenceExamples.en: He studies so hard that he is always in first place.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 아이가 어찌나 우는지 달랠 수가 없었어요.
sentenceExamples.en: That child was crying so much that I couldn't comfort them.

name: N(이)라는 N
englishMeaning: A noun called N / The thing known as N
briefDescription: Used to define or title a noun. Similar to: N(이)라고 하는 N.
featuredTranslation: This is a gift in the name of (called) friendship.
longerExplanation: This is a contraction of 'N(이)라고 하는 N'. It is used to identify a specific title, name, or abstract concept. It often adds a slightly poetic or formal nuance to the definition.

sentenceExamples.en: The emotion called love is quite complex.
Do you know the island called Dokdo?
The thing known as happiness is in a place nearby.

name: N에 비해(서)
briefDescription: Used to establish a standard of comparison between two things. Similar to: N보다 (No. 2).
featuredTranslation: It is much colder this year compared to last year.
longerExplanation: While '보다' is a direct 'than', '에 비해(서)' functions more as 'in comparison to'. It is commonly used in reports, news, or when making a logical point about a difference in size, price, or quality.

sentenceExamples.en: Compared to the effort, the result isn't good.

sentenceExamples.kr: 형에 비해서 동생은 키가 작은 편이에요.
sentenceExamples.en: Compared to the older brother, the younger one is on the shorter side.

sentenceExamples.kr: 이 식당은 가격에 비해 서비스가 아주 좋습니다.
sentenceExamples.en: Compared to the price, the service at this restaurant is very good.

name: A/V-(으)ㄹ 게 뻔하다
englishMeaning: It's obvious that... / I know for sure that...
briefDescription: Used when the speaker is certain about a negative future outcome based on current evidence.
featuredExample: 공부를 안 해서 이번 시험도 떨어질 게 뻔해요.
featuredTranslation: It's obvious I'll fail this exam too since I didn't study.
longerExplanation: This is used for strong, objective-sounding predictions. It almost always carries a negative nuance (predicting a mistake, failure, or bad situation). It translates to 'it is as clear as day that...'.

sentenceExamples.kr: 거짓말인 게 뻔한데 왜 자꾸 우겨요?
sentenceExamples.en: It's obvious that it's a lie, so why do you keep insisting?
Even if we leave now, it's obvious we'll be late.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 소식을 들으면 화를 낼 게 뻔합니다.
sentenceExamples.en: It's certain he will be angry if he hears that news.

name: A/V-기는(요)
briefDescription: Used to politely disagree with a compliment or a statement. Similar to: 별말씀을요 (You're welcome).
featuredExample: 가: 한국말 정말 잘하시네요! 나: 잘하기는요, 아직 멀었어요.
featuredTranslation: A: You speak Korean so well! B: Not really, I still have a long way to go.
longerExplanation: This is a reactive ending. When someone gives you a compliment, using '-기는요' is the standard way to show modesty. It can also be used to mildly contradict someone's assumption (e.g., 'Busy? Not really.').

sentenceExamples.kr: 가: 어제 많이 바빴지? 나: 바쁘기는요, 하루 종일 집에서 쉬었어요.
sentenceExamples.en: A: You were busy yesterday, right? B: Not really, I rested at home all day.

sentenceExamples.kr: 가: 맵지 않아? 나: 맵기는요, 하나도 안 매워요.
sentenceExamples.en: A: Isn't it spicy? B: Far from it, it's not spicy at all.

sentenceExamples.kr: 고맙기는요, 제가 한 일도 별로 없는데요.
sentenceExamples.en: No need to thank me; I didn't really do much anyway.

name: N(이)야말로
briefDescription: Used to emphasize a noun as the prime example or the most important thing.
featuredTranslation: Health indeed is the greatest asset.
longerExplanation: This particle singles out a noun and gives it supreme emphasis. It often translates to 'If we are talking about [N], then it is definitely...' or 'More than anything else, [N] is...'.

sentenceExamples.en: This is exactly the book I was looking for.
Love indeed is the power that changes the world.

sentenceExamples.kr: 가족이야말로 제가 힘들 때 힘이 되어주는 존재예요.
sentenceExamples.en: My family indeed is the existence that gives me strength when I'm having a hard time.

name: 여간 A/V-(으)ㄴ/는 것이 아니다
briefDescription: Used to emphasize that a state is extremely high by using a double negative.
featuredExample: 한국의 여름 날씨는 여간 더운 것이 아니에요.
featuredTranslation: The summer weather in Korea is not just a little hot (It's extremely hot).
longerExplanation: This is a sophisticated formal expression. '여간' usually means 'ordinarily', so 'It is not ordinarily [X]' means 'It is extraordinarily [X]'. It is always followed by a negative like '아니다' or '않다'.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 문제는 여간 어려운 것이 아닙니다.
sentenceExamples.en: That problem is extremely (not just a little) difficult.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 사람은 고집이 여간 센 것이 아니에요.
sentenceExamples.en: That person is incredibly (extraordinarily) stubborn.

sentenceExamples.kr: 유학 생활이 여간 힘든 게 아니에요.
sentenceExamples.en: Living abroad as a student is not just a little hard; it's very tough.

name: A-다고 보다 / V-ㄴ/는다고 보다
englishMeaning: To view as / To think that (Formal opinion)
briefDescription: Used to express the speaker's personal opinion or perspective formally. Similar to: -라고 생각하다.
featuredExample: 저는 이번 계획이 성공할 것이라고 봅니다.
featuredTranslation: I view this plan as likely to succeed.
longerExplanation: This is much more formal than '-고 생각하다'. It is frequently used in discussions, debates, news, and essays (TOPIK II Task 54) to state a logical conclusion or a professional stance.

sentenceExamples.kr: 환경 보호가 경제 발전보다 더 중요하다고 봅니다.
sentenceExamples.en: I view environmental protection as more important than economic development.

sentenceExamples.kr: 정부는 이 문제를 심각하게 받아들여야 한다고 봅니다.
sentenceExamples.en: I believe the government should take this issue seriously.

sentenceExamples.kr: 사람마다 기준이 다르다고 볼 수 있습니다.
sentenceExamples.en: It can be viewed that standards differ for every person.

name: V-아다(가) / 어다(가)
briefDescription: Indicates that an action is performed in one place, and then the resulting object is moved to another place.
featuredTranslation: I bought fish at the market and (brought it home and) made stew.
longerExplanation: This grammar implies a physical transfer. You perform Action A in location 1, and the result of that action is carried over to perform Action B in location 2. It is often used with buying, picking up, or making things.

sentenceExamples.kr: 꽃집에서 꽃을 사다가 방에 꽂아 두었어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I bought flowers from the shop and put them in my room.
I borrowed a book from the library and read it at home.
I folded some paper and (took it and) made a plane.

name: N을/를 비롯해서 [비롯한]
briefDescription: Used to list items while highlighting the first one as the most important or representative.
featuredExample: 서울을 비롯한 대도시의 인구 밀도가 높습니다.
featuredTranslation: The population density of large cities, starting with Seoul, is high.
longerExplanation: This formal structure is used to group items under a category. N is presented as the primary example, and the following part includes the rest of the group. It is common in news and official reports.

sentenceExamples.kr: 교장 선생님을 비롯해서 많은 선생님들이 참석하셨습니다.
sentenceExamples.en: Many teachers attended, including the principal (as the lead).

sentenceExamples.kr: 김치를 비롯한 한국 음식이 세계적으로 유명해졌어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Korean food, represented by Kimchi, has become world-famous.

sentenceExamples.kr: 가족을 비롯한 주변 사람들의 응원 덕분에 이겨냈어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I overcame it thanks to the support of people around me, starting with my family.

name: A/V-(으)며
briefDescription: Used to list two or more facts or actions. Similar to: -고 (No. 108).
featuredTranslation: He is a student and also a writer at the same time.
longerExplanation: This is a more literary and formal version of '-고'. It is often used in news, reports, and books to connect descriptions or simultaneous states. It sounds more objective and refined than '-고'.

sentenceExamples.en: The weather is clear and the wind is not blowing (Formal).

sentenceExamples.kr: 운동은 건강에 좋으며 기분 전환에도 도움이 된다.
sentenceExamples.en: Exercise is good for health and helpful for a change of pace.
She is kind and has good manners.

name: A/V-거든
briefDescription: Used to express a condition followed by a command or advice. Similar to: -(으)면 (No. 106).
featuredTranslation: Once you are ready (if you are ready), let's depart.
longerExplanation: Note: This is different from the reason ending '-거든요'. This conditional '-거든' is mostly used in spoken Korean to give a condition that must be met before a command, suggestion, or promise can take place. It is not used for simple hypothetical situations.

sentenceExamples.en: If you arrive, please call me immediately.

sentenceExamples.kr: 배가 고프거든 식탁에 있는 빵을 먹어.
sentenceExamples.en: If you're hungry, eat the bread on the table.
If you're bored, come over to my house to hang out.

name: N(이)라면
englishMeaning: If it is N / When it comes to N
briefDescription: Used for conditions involving nouns. Similar to: N(이)면.
featuredTranslation: If it's a Korean person, everyone knows him.
longerExplanation: This is the noun form of the conditional '-다면'. It is often used when making a general statement about a category (If you are a student, if it's the weekend) or when expressing a personal preference ('When it comes to coffee, I like Americano').

sentenceExamples.en: If it were me, I wouldn't have done it that way.
If it were Sunday, I would have rested at home.
If it's coffee (when it comes to coffee), I have to have an iced americano.

name: A-다고 들었다 / V-ㄴ/는다고 들었다
briefDescription: Used to report information the speaker heard from someone else. Similar to: -다던데 (No. 56).
featuredTranslation: I heard that the movie is very scary.
longerExplanation: This is a combination of indirect speech '-다고' and the verb '듣다' (to hear). It is a standard way to mention information received from a third party without indicating the specific source.

sentenceExamples.kr: 내일 비가 온다고 들었는데 우산 챙기셨어요?
sentenceExamples.en: I heard it's supposed to rain tomorrow; did you bring an umbrella?

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 회사는 복지가 아주 좋다고 들었습니다.
sentenceExamples.en: I heard that the company has very good benefits.

sentenceExamples.kr: 민수 씨가 다음 달에 유학 간다고 들었어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I heard that Minsu is going to study abroad next month.

name: A/V-고 해서
briefDescription: Used to give one representative reason out of several. Similar to: -아/어서 (No. 102).
featuredExample: 날씨도 좋고 해서 공원에 산책하러 나갔어요.
featuredTranslation: Since the weather was good (among other reasons), I went to the park for a walk.
longerExplanation: This structure is used when there are multiple reasons for an action, but the speaker only mentions one or two as representative. It implies 'this is a major reason, but there are others as well'.

sentenceExamples.kr: 피곤하기도 하고 해서 오늘은 집에서 쉬려고요.
sentenceExamples.en: I'm tired (and there are other reasons too), so I'm going to rest at home today.

sentenceExamples.kr: 배도 고프고 해서 근처 식당에 들어갔어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I was hungry (among other things), so I went into a nearby restaurant.

sentenceExamples.kr: 공부도 할 겸 친구도 만날 겸 도서관에 가요.
sentenceExamples.en: I'm going to the library both to study and to meet a friend (Similar nuance to -겸).

name: N 만에
briefDescription: Indicates that an event occurred after a certain period of time passed.
featuredTranslation: I returned to my hometown after 10 years.
longerExplanation: Used when a specific result or change happens after a certain duration has elapsed. It is often used to emphasize that a long time has passed since the last occurrence of an event.

sentenceExamples.kr: 수업 시작한 지 5분 만에 잠이 들었어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I fell asleep just 5 minutes after the class started.

sentenceExamples.kr: 헤어진 지 사흘 만에 다시 만났어요.
sentenceExamples.en: We met again only three days after breaking up.

sentenceExamples.kr: 이 책을 이틀 만에 다 읽었어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I finished reading this book in just two days.

name: N에 의하면
briefDescription: Used to cite a source of information. Similar to: N에 따르면.
featuredExample: 뉴스에 의하면 내일 태풍이 온다고 해요.
featuredTranslation: According to the news, a typhoon is coming tomorrow.
longerExplanation: This is a formal structure used primarily in reporting or academic writing to indicate where information originated (a person, the news, a book, a survey). It is usually followed by reported speech like '-다고 하다'.

sentenceExamples.kr: 조사 결과에 의하면 한국어 학습자가 늘고 있습니다.
sentenceExamples.en: According to the survey results, the number of Korean learners is increasing.

sentenceExamples.kr: 기상청에 의하면 올겨울은 매우 추울 것이라고 합니다.
sentenceExamples.en: According to the Meteorological Administration, this winter will be very cold.

sentenceExamples.kr: 전문가들의 의견에 의하면 이 계획은 실현 가능합니다.
sentenceExamples.en: According to the opinions of experts, this plan is feasible.

name: V-(으)려다(가)
briefDescription: Indicates an intended action was interrupted or changed to a different action. Similar to: -다가 (No. 73).
featuredExample: 커피를 마시려다가 배가 아파서 물을 마셨어요.
featuredTranslation: I was going to drink coffee, but my stomach hurt so I drank water instead.
longerExplanation: This combines the intention '-(으)려고 하다' with the interruption '-다가'. It describes a situation where the speaker was right on the verge of doing something but changed their mind or was stopped by an event.

sentenceExamples.kr: 전화하려다가 너무 늦은 것 같아서 안 했어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I was going to call, but it seemed too late so I didn't.

sentenceExamples.kr: 외출하려다가 비가 와서 집에 그냥 있었어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I was about to go out, but it rained so I just stayed home.
I was about to say that fact, but I held it back.

name: N마저
briefDescription: Used when something bad is added to an already bad situation. Similar to: N조차.
featuredTranslation: I lost even my one and only bag.
longerExplanation: '-마저' adds the nuance of 'even the last one left' or 'even the most unexpected thing'. It is almost always used in negative contexts where the speaker feels a sense of loss or hopelessness.

sentenceExamples.en: Even the last remaining hope has vanished.
Do even you not believe me? (of all people).
Even the house was washed away in the heavy rain.

name: N과/와 달리
briefDescription: Used to express a contrast between two nouns. Similar to: N에 비해서 (No. 216).
featuredTranslation: Unlike the older brother, the younger brother has an active personality.
longerExplanation: This structure is used to highlight a specific difference in quality, behavior, or state between two subjects. It functions as an adverbial phrase.

sentenceExamples.en: Unlike our expectations, the exam was very easy.

sentenceExamples.kr: 서울과 달리 이 도시는 조용하고 깨끗해요.
sentenceExamples.en: Unlike Seoul, this city is quiet and clean.
Unlike yesterday, the weather is clear today.

name: N에 따라(서)
englishMeaning: According to N / Depending on N
briefDescription: Indicates that the following action or result changes based on the noun.
featuredTranslation: Cultures differ depending on the country.
longerExplanation: Used to show that a situation is variable. The result in the second clause is determined by the standard or criteria set by the noun in the first clause.

sentenceExamples.kr: 사람에 따라 생각이 다를 수 있어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Thoughts can differ depending on the person.
Choose the color according to your preference.

sentenceExamples.kr: 날씨에 따라 계획이 바뀔 수도 있습니다.
sentenceExamples.en: Plans may change depending on the weather.

name: N에 불과하다
englishMeaning: Is merely N / Is nothing more than N
briefDescription: Used to downplay or belittle the amount or importance of a noun.
featuredTranslation: This is merely the beginning.
longerExplanation: This is a formal/written expression used to show that something does not exceed a certain (usually low) level or standard. It often carries a nuance of limitation.

sentenceExamples.en: That rumor is nothing more than a lie.
Merely 10% of the participants agreed.
He is merely an acquaintance to me.

name: N만 못하다
englishMeaning: Not as good as N / Inferior to N
briefDescription: Used to say that something is of lower quality or degree than N.
featuredTranslation: The younger brother is not as good as the older brother.
longerExplanation: This is a comparative structure that establishes 'N' as the superior standard. It implies that the subject fails to reach the level of N.

sentenceExamples.en: The taste is not as good as it used to be.
This movie is not as good as the original novel.

sentenceExamples.kr: 건강을 잃으면 돈은 아무것도 아닌 것만 못하다.
sentenceExamples.en: If you lose health, money is worse than having nothing (not as good as nothing).

name: V-(으)ㄹ 게 아니라
englishMeaning: Instead of doing V / Don't just V, but...
briefDescription: Suggests a better alternative to the current or planned action.
featuredExample: 걱정만 할 게 아니라 직접 가서 확인해 보세요.
featuredTranslation: Instead of just worrying, go there yourself and check.
longerExplanation: Used to correct someone's behavior or intended plan by providing a more logical or productive alternative. It usually follows with a command or suggestion.

sentenceExamples.kr: 집에만 있을 게 아니라 산책이라도 나갑시다.
sentenceExamples.en: Instead of just staying home, let's at least go for a walk.

sentenceExamples.kr: 불평할 게 아니라 해결 방법을 찾아야 해요.
sentenceExamples.en: Instead of complaining, we need to find a solution.

sentenceExamples.kr: 말만 할 게 아니라 행동으로 보여 주세요.
sentenceExamples.en: Don't just talk, show it through actions.

name: N(으)로서
briefDescription: Indicates the status, position, or qualification of a person. Similar to: N(으)로써 (Tool/Means).
featuredTranslation: As a teacher, he loves his students.
longerExplanation: '-로서' is used for people and their roles. It explains the 'hat' someone is wearing while they perform an action or hold an opinion. (Note: Do not confuse with '-(으)로써' which is used for tools or methods).

sentenceExamples.en: As a friend, I'll give you one piece of advice.
As a parent, the child's happiness is the most important.
He participated in the competition as a representative of Korea.

name: A-다기보다는, V-ㄴ/는 다기보다는
englishMeaning: Rather than calling it X / It's not so much X as Y
briefDescription: Used to say that one description is more accurate than another.
featuredTranslation: Rather than calling it scary, that movie was sad.
longerExplanation: Used when the speaker wants to refine a description. It acknowledges that the first term might be used, but the second term is a more precise or suitable fit for the situation.

sentenceExamples.en: It's not so much that I hate it as I'm just not interested.
Rather than saying I succeeded, I think I was just lucky.
It wasn't that I was busy so much as I didn't feel like going (it was bothersome).

name: 설마 A/V-겠어요?
englishMeaning: No way... right? / Surely it wouldn't...
briefDescription: Expresses strong disbelief or the hope that something negative won't happen.
featuredTranslation: Surely that rumor wouldn't be true, right?
longerExplanation: The adverb '설마' signals that the speaker finds a situation hard to believe. When paired with the presumptive '-겠어요', it seeks confirmation that the unlikely/negative event is not the reality.

sentenceExamples.kr: 설마 비가 오겠어요? 하늘이 이렇게 맑은데요.
sentenceExamples.en: Surely it won't rain? The sky is so clear.
No way you've eaten it all already, right?
Surely he haven't forgotten me?

name: N(으)로부터
briefDescription: Indicates the starting point or source. Similar to: N에게서 (No. 104 similar).
featuredTranslation: I received a gift from a friend.
longerExplanation: Used for formal situations or when describing the origin of a feeling, a piece of information, or a physical object. It is often used with inanimate sources (like organizations) but can be used for people too.

sentenceExamples.en: I want to be independent from my parents.
We came to receive support from the government.
That news was delivered from the media.

name: A-다 싶다, V-ㄴ/는 다 싶다
englishMeaning: I have a feeling that... / It seems to me that...
briefDescription: Expresses a subjective thought or an impression. Similar to: -ㄴ 것 같다 (No. 1).
featuredTranslation: I felt that this was enough, so I stopped.
longerExplanation: Used when the speaker has an inner thought or intuition. It describes a 'subjective sense' or a conclusion reached in the speaker's mind based on their perception of the situation.

sentenceExamples.en: If you have a feeling it's wrong, fix it immediately.
Feeling that it was too late, I hurried out.
Thinking it would be tasty, I tried buying one.

name: A/V-았었/었었-
briefDescription: Indicates a past state or action that is completely over and no longer exists. Similar to: -았던/었던 (No. 182).
featuredTranslation: I used to be very fat when I was young (but I'm not now).
longerExplanation: The 'double past' creates a distance between the past event and the present. It emphasizes that the state in the past is finished and is often used to contrast the past with a different current reality.

sentenceExamples.en: I lived in Korea until last year (implying I don't now).
I used to be unable to eat spicy food (implying I can now).

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 사람을 한 번 만났었었는데 기억이 안 나요.
sentenceExamples.en: I had met that person once in the past, but I don't remember.

name: V-는 사이(에)
englishMeaning: While / During the interval of V
briefDescription: Indicates that an unexpected event happened while an action was occurring. Similar to: -는 동안 (No. 122).
featuredTranslation: While I was dozing off for a moment, I passed my stop.
longerExplanation: Focuses on a short or specific interval of time during which something else happened (often unexpectedly). It can have different subjects in each clause.

sentenceExamples.kr: 엄마가 전화를 받는 사이에 아기가 울기 시작했어요.
sentenceExamples.en: While mom was answering the phone, the baby started crying.

sentenceExamples.kr: 도둑이 내가 한눈을 파는 사이에 지갑을 훔쳐갔어요.
sentenceExamples.en: The thief stole my wallet while I was looking away.
While I was resting for a bit, the rain stopped.

name: A-다는 N, V-ㄴ/는다는 N
briefDescription: Used to describe a noun using a reported statement. Similar to: -다고 하는 N.
featuredTranslation: I heard the news that there is an exam tomorrow.
longerExplanation: This is a noun-modifying form for indirect quotations. It is used when the following noun (like news, rumor, fact, promise) content is the clause that precedes it.

sentenceExamples.en: The rumor that he succeeded is widespread.
I kept the promise that we would meet again.
The fact that he is not the culprit was revealed.

name: A-(으)ㄴ지 A-(으)ㄴ지, V-는지 V-는지
briefDescription: Used to list options when the speaker is unsure. Similar to: -든지 (No. 43).
featuredTranslation: I'm not sure if he is a student or a teacher.
longerExplanation: Commonly followed by verbs of 'knowing' or 'inquiring' (모르다, 알다, 물어보다). It expresses a choice between two or more possibilities where the exact answer is unknown.

sentenceExamples.kr: 비가 오는지 안 오는지 확인해 보세요.
sentenceExamples.en: Check whether it's raining or not.
I don't know if this is correct or wrong.

sentenceExamples.kr: 어디가 아픈지 왜 아픈지 말해 봐.
sentenceExamples.en: Tell me where it hurts and why it hurts.

name: A-다는 것은 N에서/N(으)로 알 수 있다
englishMeaning: The fact that X can be seen from N
briefDescription: Formal structure used to provide evidence for a statement.
featuredExample: 그가 성실하다는 것은 그의 행동에서 알 수 있어요.
featuredTranslation: The fact that he is sincere can be seen from his actions.
longerExplanation: This is a logical concluding structure often used in essays or speeches. It presents a 'truth' in the first part and points to the 'proof' or 'source' in the second part.

sentenceExamples.kr: 한국 문화가 인기 있다는 것은 통계로 알 수 있습니다.
sentenceExamples.en: The fact that Korean culture is popular can be seen through statistics.

sentenceExamples.kr: 환경이 오염됐다는 것은 공기 상태에서 알 수 있어요.
sentenceExamples.en: The fact that the environment is polluted can be seen from the state of the air.

sentenceExamples.kr: 실력이 늘었다는 것은 시험 점수로 알 수 있습니다.
sentenceExamples.en: The fact that skills improved can be seen from the exam scores.

name: N이에요/예요
briefDescription: The basic polite ending used to identify or define a noun. Similar to: N입니다 (No. 249).
featuredTranslation: I am a student.
longerExplanation: Used to attach 'to be' to a noun in a polite, informal setting. '이에요' is used after a consonant (받침), and '예요' is used after a vowel.

sentenceExamples.en: This is my bag.
My friend is a chef.
Tomorrow is my birthday.

name: N입니다 / N입니까?
briefDescription: The formal version of the verb 'to be'. Similar to: N이에요/예요 (No. 248).
featuredTranslation: Nice to meet you. I am Kim Min-su.
longerExplanation: Used in formal situations like introductions, news, or business. '입니다' is the statement form, and '입니까?' is the question form.

sentenceExamples.en: What is your occupation?
This is Seoul Station.
That person is our teacher.

name: N이/가 아닙니다
briefDescription: The formal negation of 'to be'. Similar to: N이/가 아니에요.
featuredTranslation: I am not Japanese.
longerExplanation: Used to state that the subject is not the noun mentioned. Requires the subject particle '이/가' attached to the noun.

sentenceExamples.en: This is not my wallet.
Today is not a holiday.
That person is not a doctor.

name: N이/가 있어요/없어요
englishMeaning: To have / To exist / There is
briefDescription: Used to express possession or the existence of a noun in a location.
featuredTranslation: I have a Korean friend.
longerExplanation: Used to say 'I have [N]' or 'There is [N]'. If the noun ends in a consonant, use '이', if a vowel, use '가'.

sentenceExamples.en: The teacher is in the classroom.
I don't have an umbrella.
Do you have time?

name: N 주세요
briefDescription: A basic polite way to request a noun (items/food). Similar to: V-아/어 주세요 (Requesting an action).
featuredTranslation: Please give me some water.
longerExplanation: The standard way to order food or ask for an item in a shop. It combines the noun with '주다' (to give) in the polite imperative form.

sentenceExamples.en: Please give me the menu.
Please give me one roll of kimbap.
Please give me three apples.

name: N하고, N과/와
briefDescription: Used to connect two nouns. Similar to: N(이)랑 (No. 119 similar).
featuredTranslation: I ate bread and milk.
longerExplanation: '하고' is common in speech. '과/와' is slightly more formal; '과' follows a consonant, '와' follows a vowel.

sentenceExamples.en: I watched a movie with a friend yesterday.
There are desks and chairs in the classroom.
My sibling and I are very different.

name: V-아요/어요
briefDescription: The standard polite present tense ending for verbs and adjectives.
featuredTranslation: I am going home now.
longerExplanation: Used to describe current actions or general facts. If the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, use '-아요'. For all other vowels, use '-어요'. 하요 becomes 해요.

sentenceExamples.en: I am eating lunch.
The weather is good today.
I study Korean every day.

name: N에서
briefDescription: Indicates the place where an action occurs. Similar to: N에 (Location of existence).
featuredTranslation: I study at the library.
longerExplanation: Unlike '에', which marks where something *is*, '에서' marks where something *happens*.

sentenceExamples.en: I meet a friend at a restaurant.
I bought clothes at the department store.
I am resting at home.

name: 안 V
briefDescription: The short form of negation. Similar to: -지 않다 (No. 11).
featuredTranslation: I don't eat meat.
longerExplanation: Placing '안' before a verb or adjective makes it negative. For 'Noun+하다' verbs, '안' goes between the noun and '하다' (e.g., 공부 안 해요).

sentenceExamples.en: I am not going to school today.
The movie is not interesting.
I was tired, so I didn't do my homework.

name: N에 (Destination)
briefDescription: Used with motion verbs (go, come) to indicate the destination.
featuredTranslation: I go to the mountain on the weekend.
longerExplanation: Attached to a location noun when used with verbs like 가다, 오다, 다니다.

sentenceExamples.en: When are you coming to Korea?
I go to the office (commute) every day.
Where do you want to go?

name: N 앞, 뒤, 옆, 위, 밑
englishMeaning: In front, Behind, Beside, On, Under
briefDescription: Spatial nouns used to indicate precise location. Similar to: N 근처 (Nearby).
featuredTranslation: There is a convenience store in front of the school.
longerExplanation: These nouns specify position and are almost always followed by the location particle '에'.

sentenceExamples.en: The book is on the desk.
There is a pharmacy beside the bank.
The puppy is sleeping under the bed.

name: N에 (Time)
briefDescription: Indicates the time when a certain action or state occurs. Similar to: -ㄹ 때 (No. 130).
featuredTranslation: I wake up at 8 AM.
longerExplanation: Attached to nouns of time like hours, days, months, and years. (Note: Do not use with 'today', 'tomorrow', or 'yesterday').

sentenceExamples.en: I will meet a friend on Sunday.
My birthday is in December.
I can't sleep at night.

name: N 개, 번, 명, 권
briefDescription: Nouns used with Native Korean numbers to count items.
featuredTranslation: Give me two apples, please.
longerExplanation: Korean uses specific counters for different objects. 개 (items), 번 (times), 명 (people), 권 (books), 병 (bottles), 잔 (glasses/cups).

sentenceExamples.en: There are four people in my family.
I want to drink a cup of coffee.
I read this book three times.

name: N도
briefDescription: Used to add the meaning of 'also' to a noun.
featuredTranslation: I like apples and I also like bananas.
longerExplanation: Replaces particles like 이/가 or 을/를 to indicate that the noun is being added to a previous statement.

sentenceExamples.en: I am a student too.
Are you busy tomorrow too?
I can also speak Korean.

name: A/V-습니다 / ㅂ니다
briefDescription: The standard ending for formal and official contexts. Similar to: -아요/어요 (No. 254).
featuredTranslation: I study hard (Formal).
longerExplanation: Used in the military, business, news, and when addressing a large public audience. It conveys maximum respect and social distance.

sentenceExamples.en: The weather is hot (Formal).
What are you looking for? (Formal)
The food is very delicious (Formal).

name: A/V-네요
briefDescription: Used to express surprise or realization upon discovering a fact.
featuredTranslation: The baby is so cute!
longerExplanation: Used when you personally see, feel, or experience something for the first time and want to exclaim about it. It’s like saying 'Wow, it's really [X]!'

sentenceExamples.en: You speak Korean quite well!
Wow, it's already 12 o'clock.
Look, it's snowing.

name: N(의) N
briefDescription: Indicates that the second noun belongs to or is related to the first noun.
featuredTranslation: This is my book.
longerExplanation: Attached to a noun to show possession. In speech, '나의' becomes '내', '저의' becomes '제', and '너의' becomes '네'. The particle '의' is often pronounced as '에'.
